metadata.title: Week 2 Progress
metadata.narration_policy: Narration is SCRIPT.md verbatim, one script section per beat: B00 = section 1, B01-B07 = sections 2-8, BOUT = section 9.
metadata.visual_policy: Simple illustrative Manim cards in the humanitarians palette, in the same style as the Week 4 progress video. No photos or recordings of the fellow, no person icons, no real company, product or tool logos; tools named in the narration are shown as generic drawn shapes or plain text. Any file, terminal, browser or video frame shown is drawn, not a screenshot.
metadata.structure_note: Same simple structure as the Week 4 progress video: Claude composer cold open, seven body cards, logo outro. No hesitant-writer, verdict or Your Turn beats, because the narration is the fellow's script exactly and the script has no lines for them.

portrait_layout.rule: In 9:16, all text and labels sit above 86% of the frame height (y < 0.86 * H), leaving the bottom 14% empty. Portrait type is large and labels are short.

metadata.fill_rule: Gate V needs content covering at least 55% of the safe area at 50% and at 85% of every beat. Each scene lays out its full cast early and holds it.
metadata.library_check: Searched with ./art scenes first: failing checks, frozen render, folder of files, done versus pass, timeline of beats, terminal prompt. See SHOTLIST.md. Reused: ClaudeComposerAsk / ClaudeComposerAsk916 and LogoOutro / LogoOutro916; B01-B07 are custom Manim.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Keya, and this is my week two progress update for the Brutalist project, where I'm learning to create videos as code. The voice you're hearing is an AI voice reading my script.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hi, Keya'
three result lines land: week 2 progress, what I built and fixed, what I learned
the AI-voice disclosure is spoken while the answered composer holds

props.command: Help me share my week: the video I made, what I fixed, and what I learned.

beats.narration_text: This week's explainer is Will AI Replace My Test Scripts? It comes from my own work writing Selenium tests. I researched self-healing locators and AI testing agents, wrote the script, and built the video with Claude Code. I also checked some Brutalist videos, and spent time choosing topics that matter to me and that I'm interested in.

show.event: title card for the explainer
my own work with Selenium tests
self-healing locators and AI testing agents
wrote the script and built with Claude Code
a video checked
three topic cards, two starred

shot.visual_intent: Title card for the explainer; my own work with selenium tests; self-healing locators and ai testing agents; wrote the script and built with claude code; a video checked; three topic cards, two starred.

beats.narration_text: In the first days, my Manim scenes kept failing the quality checks: code that wouldn't run, labels outside the safe area, and frames that were too empty. Some Remotion renders froze for over an hour. We fixed each scene instead of switching the checks off, and ran Remotion with a different browser and a time limit.

show.event: three failing-check cards (code, safe area, empty frame)
a Remotion render frozen on a clock
each scene fixed with checks left on
a different browser
a time limit

shot.visual_intent: Three failing-check cards (code, safe area, empty frame); a remotion render frozen on a clock; each scene fixed with checks left on; a different browser; a time limit.

beats.narration_text: I also learned what each file in a video folder does. The script holds my words. The beat sheet times every moment. The fact check ties each claim to a source. And the build state records whether the video really passed.

show.event: four dashed slots fill with script, beat sheet, fact check and build state, then a tick

shot.visual_intent: Four dashed slots fill with script, beat sheet, fact check and build state, then a tick.

beats.narration_text: That taught me something important. A command that says done, or even pass, isn't proof. Once, a pass came from old frames. Now I check build-state.json, which records the real result.

show.event: a terminal says done, then pass, marked 'not proof'
old frames carry a PASS stamp
build-state.json shown with an eye and a 'real result' badge

shot.visual_intent: A terminal says done, then pass, marked 'not proof'; old frames carry a pass stamp; build-state.json shown with an eye and a 'real result' badge.

beats.narration_text: Near the end, I changed my intro line. Because the narration is the clock, only that one beat needed new audio and a new render. Everything else stayed exactly the same.

show.event: an intro line is edited
the narration is the clock
one beat block marked new audio and new render
the other blocks tick as unchanged

shot.visual_intent: An intro line is edited; the narration is the clock; one beat block marked new audio and new render; the other blocks tick as unchanged.

beats.narration_text: The hard part was getting used to coding with AI in the terminal: prompting clearly for what I expect, and making sure I understand each step, not just approving it. It's only week two, and I'm still learning.

show.event: a terminal prompt with 'what I expect'
steps ticked with an eye on each
an Approve button crossed at its corner
a progress bar 'week two: still learning'

shot.visual_intent: A terminal prompt with 'what i expect'; steps ticked with an eye on each; an approve button crossed at its corner; a progress bar 'week two: still learning'.

beats.narration_text: Like the testing agents in my video, Claude Code does the work, but I still decide what correct looks like.

show.event: three cards in turn: testing agents (look, act, check), Claude Code does the work, I decide what correct looks like

shot.visual_intent: Three cards in turn: testing agents (look, act, check), claude code does the work, i decide what correct looks like.
